title: Investigating the Social Media & Adolescent Well-Being Paradox

questions.question: Scenario: Dr. Ellis conducts a cross-sectional study on 2,000 high school students and finds a statistically significant negative correlation (r = -0.32, p < 0.001) between daily Instagram screen time and self-reported emotional well-being. A tech blog reports: 'Instagram directly destroys teenage happiness.' What is the fundamental methodological flaw in this headline?

options.text: It infers a causal relationship from a cross-sectional correlational design without establishing temporal precedence or ruling out third variables
The sample size of 2,000 is far too small for statistical significance
Negative correlations can never be statistically significant
Instagram cannot be measured on a ratio scale

questions.explanation: A cross-sectional correlation shows an association, but cannot establish that screen time causes diminished well-being; unhappy teens might seek out more screen time (reverse directionality), or family conflict could drive both.

questions.question: Dr. Ellis recruited all 2,000 participants by posting a link on her university lab's public Twitter account. What sampling bias threatens the external validity of her findings?

options.text: Simple random sampling bias
Self-selection convenience bias (volunteers who follow a psychology Twitter account differ systematically from the general adolescent population)
Stratified cluster error
The Hawthorne effect

questions.explanation: Using an online volunteer link on Twitter selects a self-selected convenience sample that is not representative of all adolescents.

questions.question: To operationalize 'emotional well-being', Dr. Ellis created a 10-item Likert survey. She calculates Cronbach's alpha as α = 0.88. What psychometric conclusion can she draw from this metric?

options.text: The scale has strong internal consistency reliability
The scale has proven predictive criterion validity
The scale has zero measurement error
The scale represents a ratio level of measurement

questions.explanation: A Cronbach's alpha of 0.88 confirms that the items on the scale consistently measure the same underlying conceptual construct.

questions.question: When Dr. Ellis statistically controls for 'nighttime sleep disruption' using a partial correlation, the correlation between social media use and low well-being drops from r = -0.32 to r = -0.04 (non-significant). What does this reveal?

options.text: Sleep disruption was a confounding third variable explaining the initial correlation
The study committed scientific fraud
Social media use causes permanent brain damage
The measurement scale changed from ordinal to interval

questions.explanation: When controlling for sleep eliminates the correlation, it demonstrates that sleep loss was the confounding mediator/third variable driving the apparent relationship.

questions.question: Because the participants were 15-year-old high school students, what ethical protocol was legally and procedurally required before collecting their data?

options.text: Only the student's verbal agreement was required
Informed consent from parents or legal guardians, along with the adolescent's developmental assent
A waiver of all ethical oversight signed by the school principal
Submission to an IACUC animal committee

questions.explanation: Minors cannot legally provide informed consent; parents or legal guardians must provide consent, and minors must provide assent.

questions.question: To establish temporal precedence without a laboratory intervention, what longitudinal research design should Dr. Ellis deploy?

options.text: A cross-lagged panel design tracking both screen time and well-being at 6-month intervals across 2 years
A single-case study of one depressed teenager
An anonymous web poll with 100,000 clicks
A naturalistic observation of a computer lab for 10 minutes

questions.explanation: A cross-lagged panel design measures both variables repeatedly across time to determine whether screen time predicts subsequent well-being or vice versa.
